claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a homogeneous, non-equilibrium metastable solid solution.
During service, the metastable solid solution undergoes diffusion-controlled decomposition.
Decomposition produces nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-containing lightweight HEAs have a tendency to develop intermetallic or complex secondary phases.
The precipitates nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Intermetallic precipitation causes local elemental depletion or enrichment in the residual matrix.
Local segregation changes the formation and stability of protective oxide scales and passivation layers.
Retention of critical oxide-forming elements permits high-temperature oxidation resistance to be retained.
Depletion of passivating or protective-oxide-forming elements promotes non-protective oxides and greater corrosion susceptibility.
Aged samples will develop a heterogeneous microstructure containing discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Aged samples will develop compositional gradients relative to the initially uniform state.
Changes in corrosion and oxidation resistance will correlate systematically with the precipitation and segregation process.
Aging at approximately 400–600 °C can permit the proposed diffusion-controlled microstructural changes.
The predictive regime requires sufficient temperature and duration for intermetallic nucleation but excludes complete phase homogenization.
Very high temperatures or very long exposures can cause full transformation or saturation of secondary phases.
The original baseline alloy is rapidly solidified, metastable, single-phase, and compositionally uniform.
Transformation kinetics and the balance between intermetallic formation and protective-element preservation vary with composition and processing history.
Absence of significant intermetallic development and segregation, or absence of a systematic relationship between those changes and resistance, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
